    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Those three letters on a semi-truck usually refer to long-distance driving.
    • Industry observers note that trucks are full of weird and useful features that most people overlook without knowing their real purpose.
    • What can look like a government code can have a specific meaning in the trucking industry.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Those three letters on a semi-truck usually refer to long-distance driving. Learn what OTR means and how different trucking routes work.

    Industry observers note that trucks are full of weird and useful features that most people overlook without knowing their real purpose. Some have long spikes on their wheels. Others might feature amber lights on top. You might even see diamond shaped signs. But what about OTR written on a truck?

    What can look like a government code can have a specific meaning in the trucking industry. Learn what OTR means, how long-haul work compares with shorter routes, and why the context matters.

    In trucking, OTR stands for “over-the-road.” It refers to long-haul trucking, where drivers transport freight across long distances, often through several states or into Canada. According to trucking tech giant Schneider, OTR drivers can spend weeks away from home. Many drive trucks with sleeper cabs that provide a place to rest between shifts.

    It has been revealed that OTR describes the type of work, not a specific truck. It’s also not a required marking. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires certain identifying information, including a tech giant’s name and USDOT number, on interstate commercial trucks, but OTR isn’t part of that requirement.

    In a recent development, the letters can also mean something different depending on where they appear. In the tire industry, OTR stands for “off-the-road,” referring to heavy-duty tires used on construction and mining equipment. OTR Diagnostics is also the name of a maintenance tool that helps truck owners check engine problems and other vehicle information.

    OTR truck drivers transport freight over long distances, often making several stops along the way. Their jobs can also involve inspecting their trucks, handling delivery paperwork, and sometimes helping load or unload cargo.

    Recent findings suggest that because these trips can last for weeks, drivers often sleep in their trucks or stop at other places along their routes. The FMCSA limits how long commercial drivers can drive without taking required breaks and rest periods.

    Drivers who operate most full-size tractor-trailers need a Class A commercial driver’s license (CDL). Depending on the organization and route, drivers may spend several weeks working before returning home.

    OTR drivers cover the longest distances and may spend weeks away from home. Regional drivers work within a particular area of the country, often returning home weekly or more frequently. Local drivers generally stay closer to home and return after each shift, although they can still work long hours.

    There’s also dedicated trucking, where drivers regularly transport freight for the same customer or between the same locations. These routes can be local, regional, or long-distance, depending on the firm.

    The exact distances and schedules vary between employers, so the terms don’t always describe the same mileage or amount of time away from home.

    Schneider, “Over-the-Road (OTR) Truck Driving Jobs” Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, “How Do I Get a Commercial Driver’s License?” OTR Performance, “Why Choose OTR Diagnostics?“.

    #8508. Latest Update: School Board Can Order High School Teacher to Remove "Hate Has No Home Here" Rainbow Poster

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1019 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: School Board Can Order High School Teacher to Remove "Hate Has No Home Here" Rainbow Poster

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1019 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Little Miami School Dist., decided Monday by Judge Matthew McFarland (S.D.
    • Plaintiff George McIntyre is a teacher at Little Miami High School, a school within Defendant Little Miami School District ("District"), where he teaches American History and Advanced Placement European History.
    • As shown above, the Poster features five hands holding hearts filled with distinct symbols, including the American flag, a peace sign, the rainbow pride flag, and the transgender pride flag.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    From McIntyre v. Little Miami School Dist., decided Monday by Judge Matthew McFarland (S.D. Ohio) (appeal pending):.

    Plaintiff George McIntyre is a teacher at Little Miami High School, a school within Defendant Little Miami School District ("District"), where he teaches American History and Advanced Placement European History. McIntyre placed a poster in his classroom displaying the slogan "Hate Has No Home Here" ("Poster"), depicted below:.

    As shown above, the Poster features five hands holding hearts filled with distinct symbols, including the American flag, a peace sign, the rainbow pride flag, and the transgender pride flag. McIntyre hung up the Poster to remind his students to "treat all their classmates with mutual respect, regardless of personal opinions or beliefs." ….

    Industry observers note that the District's "longstanding practice" has been to permit teachers to decorate their classrooms and display personal items. That latitude, however, is "defined by" the District's Little Miami School Board ("Board") policy.

    It has been revealed that that policy landscape shifted when the Ohio General Assembly enacted House Bill 8, known as the Ohio Parents' Bill of Rights. That statute requires school districts to provide parental notice and review for materials containing "sexuality content" and allows parents to opt out for alternative assignments. "[S]exuality content" is defined as "oral or written instruction, presentation, image, or description of sexual concepts or gender ideology in a classroom setting," but explicitly excludes "[i]ncidental references to sexual concepts or gender ideology occurring outside of formal instruction or presentations on such topics." On October 28, 2025, the Board adopted Board Policy 5780.01, incorporating the statute's definitions and notice/opt-out requirements into District policy.

    The Board considered restricting classroom wall-hangings exclusively to the U.S. flag, the Ohio flag, and school-related displays, but ultimately concluded that state law and Board Policy 5780.01 provided sufficient oversight. Under District guidance, concerns that a classroom display contains "sexuality content" under state law or Board Policy 5780.01 are subject to a three-tiered review: first by the school principal, then on appeal to the superintendent, and finally to the Board….

    In September 2025, Defendant David Wallace, the Board President, visited McIntyre's classroom and photographed the Poster. Thereafter, Wallace contacted District Superintendent Regina Morgan, requesting that McIntyre remove the Poster. Morgan relayed the request to Little Miami High School's Principal, Kevin Harleman.

    Harleman spoke with McIntyre about the Poster, and asked whether McIntyre tied the display to his curriculum or classroom discussions, or if it was simply a decorative wall hanging. On February 2, 2026, McIntyre emailed Harleman, identifying specific content standards within the model curriculum for his classes that he felt the Poster was "especially applicable" to. McIntyre further noted that, while the Poster applied to those broad historical themes, it was not used as a formal instructional device and instead was "a reminder that [his students] must treat their classmates with mutual respect." Harleman forwarded that email to Morgan.

    The next day, Morgan informed Wallace that, upon her review, while the Poster contained sexual identity symbols, she did not "believe a reasonable observer would conclude its primary purpose [was] to prompt discussion, provide instruction, or solicit student engagement on sexual concepts or gender ideology." Under the "display guidelines," Morgan acknowledged that it was "now a Board decision as to how to move forward." ….

    [On February 25, t]he Board voted 4 to 1 to classify the Poster as sexuality content under Board Policy 5780.01 and ordered its immediate removal from McIntyre's classroom….

    The court rejected McIntyre's claim that the Board's actions violated his First Amendment rights:.

    Although public employees "undoubtably enjoy certain rights," those rights "do not transform them into 'sovereigns unto themselves.'" Rather, "the government, just like a private employer, retains 'control over what the employer itself has commissioned or created': the employee's job." That authority carries particular significance in the context of public education, where Ohio's compulsory-attendance requirements give public school teachers "a captive audience for their in-class speech." ….

    Recent findings suggest that [Thus], the Sixth Circuit has held that a public school teacher's in-class curricular and pedagogical choices are not protected by the First Amendment. In reaching this holding, the Sixth Circuit reasoned that "[w]hen a teacher teaches, the school system does not regulate that speech as much as it hires that speech. Expression is a teacher's stock in trade, the commodity [ ]he sells to [his] employer in exchange for a salary." Since Ohio law left curriculum choices to elected school boards as "an accountability measure," those boards are entitled to "regulate the content of what is or is not expressed" on their behalf….

    Here, McIntyre spoke as a public employee pursuant to his official duties when displaying the Poster in his classroom. McIntyre hung the Poster to foster a respectful environment among his students and later identified specific state curriculum standards that he believed the Poster supported…. McIntyre's motivations and actions were directly related to, and arose from his professional responsibilities as a teacher shaping his students' learning environment.

    According to recent reports, whether McIntyre used the Poster for formal instruction is immaterial. He gained access to and control over the classroom wall space through his position as a public school employee, not as a private citizen. His ability to maintain classroom displays thus existed within the scope of that public employment, which the Board regulated through established policies. As McIntyre displayed the Poster pursuant to his official duties, his expression constituted unprotected employee speech.

    Contrary to McIntyre's argument, the Supreme Court's holding in Kennedy v. Bremerton School Dist. (2022) does not alter this conclusion. Unlike the high school coach in Kennedy, who offered a brief prayer while essentially "off the clock" after a game, McIntyre maintained a permanent display on his classroom wall that was visible during school hours. Managing the classroom environment during the school day relates to his job responsibilities, not private citizen speech. Kennedy thus does not compel a finding that McIntyre spoke as a private citizen…. The Board was [thus] entitled to restrain [McIntyre's] speech, and McIntyre is not entitled to declaratory judgment that his First Amendment rights were violated….

    Omar Tarazi represents defendants.

    Is a Reverse Osmosis Filter System Actually Worth It? We Break Down Every Cost

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, what’s lurking in your water?
    • Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
    • In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    In a recent development, what’s lurking in your water? RO filters get rid of everything from microplastics to heavy metals, but are they overkill?

    Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

    In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.

    Sources indicate that I’ve lived in some places with questionable drinking water. One town issued a notice that the municipal water supply had experienced a sewage incident. Another had an arsenic problem. I’ve also lived on well water, with concerns of contamination from nearby agricultural fields.

    My solution used to be buying five-gallon jugs of spring water. But that was costly and a hassle, so six years ago, I switched to an under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) filter for my drinking and cooking water.

    Sources indicate that under-sink RO filters work like this: water passes through a series of filters, including an RO membrane, which removes dissolved substances — including lead, arsenic, nitrates, forever chemicals, chlorine, fluoride and sediment — down to 0.0001 microns. The cleaned water then comes out through a faucet, installed near the sink.

    “Reverse osmosis provides the safest level of drinking water possible,” indicates international water filtration specialist Andrew D. Daily. “It strips out 100% of bacteria, cysts, dissolved solids, chlorine, rust, viruses and microplastics.”.

    Recent findings suggest that but RO systems are also a considerable investment. So, we asked a range of health and plumbing experts for their thoughts on who should get an RO system, plus how to pick the right one. Ahead is what they said, how much RO systems cost up front and over time, and whether it’s worth the upgrade.

    RO water systems range from a few hundred dollars to over $1,000. The good news is that if you have basic plumbing knowledge and are comfortable drilling a hole in your countertop, installing one can be a DIY task. Otherwise, pro installation usually runs upwards of $300, not including add-ons like a refrigerator/ice-maker connection, leak protection, an additional electric outlet and other plumbing modifications.

    According to recent reports, the biggest downside to RO systems is that they waste water. For every gallon that comes out of the faucet, somewhere between one-half and four gallons get flushed down the drain through the filtration process. That means if you use 5 gallons of water a day for cooking and drinking, the RO system wastes between 2.5 and 20 gallons.

    Sources indicate that over a year, that adds up to between 500 and 8,500 gallons, depending on your RO system. On the low end, that’s only a few pennies more on your yearly water utility bill, but on the high end, it could be close to $100.

    Some RO water systems also require electricity. The amount of power they consume varies by model, but usually falls between 20 and 40 watts per hour. Since RO systems typically run for less than an hour a day, even if you live in a place with high electricity rates, they should add only a few dollars a year to your electricity bill.

    Maintaining RO systems is an easy DIY task, though some people choose to pay a pro to keep track of it for them. Expect to spend roughly the following for DIY maintenance:.

    Daily recommends buying only name-brand filters, even though they’re more expensive. “Name brands follow strict regulations,” he notes. ”Generic China-based deals often do not provide the same protection.”.

    It has been revealed that A quality RO system can last 10 years or longer with proper maintenance. “Many parts, including filters, membranes, faucets and tanks can be replaced individually,” says plumbing expert Danielle Smith. “Once a system gets older, though, replacement may make more sense than repeated repairs.”.

    In a recent development, “The biggest thing for me is convenience,” claims environmental and wellness expert Helen Christoni, who has an AquaTru system. “We use water all day long, drinking it, cooking with it and filling water bottles. Once installed, it just became part of my kitchen and my family’s daily health.”.

    Herman Hartanto, founder of Tampa Fast Home Buyer, has a Waterdrop G3P600 in his kitchen ($429 retail). It’s a tankless model, a feature he appreciates since it takes up minimal cabinet space. He also likes the display with real-time reports on total dissolved solids (TDS) and filter health. His only complaint is the occasional noise it generates. “The pump that draws the water on demand makes quite loud noise, which I can feel clearly at night when everything is silent,” he states.

    Recent findings suggest that personally, I’ve used two RO filter systems. My first one was an iSpring, which I chose because of its affordability. It worked well, but like Hartanto, I found the pump noisy (even though mine had a water-holding tank). My second one, which I’ve only recently installed, is a Waterdrop X12 Pro, which I chose to upgrade to because of its water-saving efficiency, ability to add calcium and magnesium back into the water, clear display and range of other premium features. So far, I’ve found it to be quiet, efficient, and free of quirks (though at $1,400 off-sale, the price is a bit of a shocker).

    Depending on what type of contaminants you have in your water, there are several alternatives to an under-sink RO water filter:.

    “Find out what’s in your water before buying anything,” notes Smith. “Don’t choose a system based only on how many stages it has or how many contaminants the box says it removes. Instead, start with your water and choose the system around what you actually need.”.

    If you’re worried about contaminants like microplastics, arsenic, lead, forever chemicals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, then an RO filter is a good choice.

    “Water quality can vary tremendously depending on where you live, and even your home’s plumbing can affect what ultimately comes out of your faucet,” indicates Christoni. “Reverse osmosis addresses such a broad range of contaminants, and with an under-sink system, that purified water is available all day long without having to think about it.”.

    Industry observers note that for Daily, the biggest reason to invest in a RO system is microplastics. “The amount of microplastics found in human brains, blood and organs have been increasing yearly,” he indicates. “Although there is not enough information to prove a detrimental effect on our health, many of my clients choose a cautious approach to water treatment.”.

    Otherwise, Daily indicates that RO filters are overkill in most U.S. cities, where tap water is generally considered safe. Even in Mexico, where water is often contaminated, he usually recommends sticking with under-sink ultrafiltration systems, since they’re a fraction of the cost, don’t waste water and don’t require power or space for a reservoir.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re presently buying bottled water, then yes, an RO system will soon pay for itself. But, otherwise, it really just depends on what you want to remove from your water. If you have arsenic, nitrates, salts, microplastics, fluoride, sulfates and other dissolved solids (TDS), RO systems are a great solution.

    According to recent reports, otherwise, a less-expensive ultrafiltration system might be a better choice. Either way, having an under-sink filtration system is a good way to ensure your family has access to clean water, both on a daily basis and after flooding events and other natural disasters that contaminate city and well water.

    So, are you ready for the upgrade?

    #8505. Breaking: The President Nominates Circuit Judges, Not Senators

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (756 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: The President Nominates Circuit Judges, Not Senators

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There has been a momentous shift in the relationship between the President and the Senate, and most people have missed it.
    • Industry observers note that let's start with the Eighth Circuit.
    • Apparently there were some discussions between the President and Boozman, and the President folded.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There has been a momentous shift in the relationship between the President and the Senate, and most people have missed it.

    Industry observers note that let's start with the Eighth Circuit. The Trump Administration interviewed Justice Cody Hiland, but determined he was not up to the task of being a circuit judge, so they offered him a federal district court seat as a consolation prize. Hiland shot back at the White House Counsel and refused the seat. He even wanted to rub it in Trump's face. The White House made a stellar nomination with Judge Lee Rudofsky. Hiland then told an entire room of law students about his experience as a lesson that should be learned. But Hiland had a friend in a high place. Senator Boozman of Arkansas lobbied Senator Tillis of North Carolina and Senator Cornyn of Texas to block Judge Rudofsky.

    Apparently there were some discussions between the President and Boozman, and the President folded. Maybe Trump determined that he needed as many judges confirmed before January, so the identity of the judge didn't matter. Maybe Trump didn't want to create more problems with his caucus. Maybe Trump just didn't care. Who knows? Trump withdrew Rudofsky and nominated Hiland. There is no guarantee that Hiland gets a hearing and makes it through the process. We are so late in the game. And frankly, I wouldn't blame some of the other conservative senators from the Eighth Circuit for putting Hiland through the paces at the hearing. It's not clear to me he'll be able to answer all the questions. But regardless of what happens, Senator Boozman won and President Trump lost.

    Sources indicate that now, onto my home, the Fifth Circuit. It is painfully clear there was some sort of deal between Judge Southwick and Senator Wicker. In no universe would the White House have picked Todd Butler without that deal. I've yet to hear anyone provide me a single shred of evidence that he is conservative beyond saying "All southern lawyers are conservative. Plus he's a Christian." What about Nathan Johnson and James Talarico? Moreover, Southwick confirmed on September 29 that he would take Senior Status, making it virtually impossible for another nominee to be selected.

    Yesterday, I watched Butler's confirmation hearing with interest. He received a few softballs from Senator Grassley, a very warm welcome from Senator Kennedy, and some surprisingly nice questions from Senator Booker about representing police officers. Butler did not seem to understand departmentalism and mis-cited Marbury v. Madison. His answers were not particularly articulate--roughly on par with his oral argument before the Supreme Court. There was no depth or curiosity conveyed. I actually think Butler tripped up on Senator Blumenthal's questions about January 6 and the election, but it didn't matter. He sailed through. Members of the conservative legal movement have raised doubts about Butler. But there were no tough questions asked by Senators Cruz, Lee, Hawley, Schmidt, or others. Only they know why they stayed out. Senator Wicker prevailed, and the President lost.

    Recent findings suggest that then there is the bizarre situation in Oklahoma. Someone yesterday asked me if I knew what Senator Armstrong was doing. My response was, "Who is Senator Armstrong?" He is the temporary senator appointed to fill Senator Mullins's seat. As Mike Fragoso relays, Armstrong is blocking the nomination of Zach West to the District Court in Oklahoma. This is all about some sort of squabble between West and defeated-AG Drummond. Armstrong returned a blue slip but is now trying to take it back. That's not how things work. If Armstrong prevails here, the President will lose.

    Recent findings suggest that circuit seats belong to the circuit, and not to the state. It bothers me that "home state" senators introduce circuit court nominees. That pageantry reinforces the wrong message. Hiland's seat does not belong to Arkansas and Butler's seat does not belong to Mississippi.

    It has been revealed that unfortunately, Trump's surrender here has created a terrible precedent. Should the Republicans ever again return to power, I would hope this entire process is reconsidered. Circuit court nominees should be treated as "at large" seats. Senators can make recommendations, but they cannot dictate who is picked. Worse, judges (like Southwick) should not be allowed to make these deals. We should not tolerate incentive structure where motivated actors can control who represents an entire circuit. Maybe the better approach is to start consulting with all the Senators in a given circuit on possible picks, and then pick the best athlete.

    Step Up Your Game With a DIY Folding Step Stool

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.
    • Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature.
    • Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.

    Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

    Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.

    Sources indicate that at some point in our lives we will need a folding step stool. You know, the one that stays out of the way but, gives you that little extra boost when you don’t need a full step ladder. In my case, I find myself reaching for a step stool more often than I’d like to admit especially when trying to reach into a work truck. When I need something, I prefer to make it and am happy to share the steps with you. Just because it is small doesn’t mean it isn’t as satisfying to make – enjoy!

    According to recent reports, on the miter saw and/or table saw, cut the top step (A), all four legs (B), the guides (C), ad the bottom crossbrace (E). Set aside everything but the legs (B) until later.

    DAN ROBERTS FOR FAMILY HANDYMAN.

    Using a compass with a pencil, draw 1-1/2-inch diameter half-circles at the bottom of each leg (B) to match the 1/2-inch width of the leg.

    Use a disc or belt sander with a coarse-grit sandpaper (80 or 100-grit) to shape the ends of the legs by sanding up to the marked pencil lines for your arch. Once you have sanded to the line, work your way up to 220-grit sandpaper for a smoother finish.

    DAN ROBERTS FOR FAMILY HANDYMAN.

    Using a router table or a router equipped with a 1/4-inch round-over bit, round over all the edges of the step (A) and all four legs (B). Be sure to use clamps to hold the pieces while making your passes with the router.

    With all the parts machined, sand all the components to 220 grit and apply a couple of coats of a wood finish of your choice. Allow the finish to dry before moving on to assembly.

    DAN ROBERTS FOR FAMILY HANDYMAN.

    Spread wood glue in hole 3 at the top of each inside leg (B). Insert the ends of the 3/4-in. dowel cross brace (D) and tap the legs on with a rubber mallet until D is fully seated.

    Recent findings suggest that set the 1-1/4-in.-square cross brace (E) between the bottoms of the legs, with its bottom edge 2-1/8 in. up from the bottom of the legs. To keep the legs parallel while you drill, clamp a scrap the same length as the cross brace (E) between them at mid-height. Check for square.

    Using hole 4 in each leg as a guide, drill a 1/2-in. hole about 1 in. deep into the center of each end of the cross brace (E). Glue 1/2-in. dowels, cut longer than the holes are deep, and drive them through the legs with a mallet until they bottom out in the cross brace (E).

    Lock each of the four joints with a single brad nail through the leg into the dowel. Trim the protruding ends of all the dowels flush with a pull saw.

    dan Roberts for family handyman.

    Flip the top step (A) upside down. Position the guide rails (C) 1/2-in. in from each side and centered front to back, leaving 1-1/2-in. at the front and back. Trace around each rail.

    Industry observers note that drill two 1/4-in. holes, 3/4-in. deep, centered on each outline. Keep the bit plumb when drilling (or drill at the drill press).

    It has been revealed that insert dowel centers in the holes. Align each rail with its outline and press down to mark the hole locations. Drill matching 1/4-in. holes in the rails, about 7/8-in. deep. That’s slightly deeper than the dowel needs, which leaves room for glue.

    Glue and insert 1/4-in x 1-1/2-in. dowels and secure the guide rails (C) to the step (A).

    dan roberts for family handyman.

    Recent findings suggest that thread 1/4-inch x 3-1/2-inch carriage bolts through hole 1 in the center of the legs to connect an outside leg to the outside of each of the connected inside legs. Put a washer between each pair of legs and secure with a nylon lock nut on the inside of the inside legs.

    DAN ROBERTS FOR FAMILY HANDYMAN.

    In a recent development, connect the two outside legs (B) to the sides of the guide rails (C) by threading 1/4-inch x 2-1/2-inch pan head screws through hole 5 in the guide rails and through hole 2 on the outside legs. Use a washer on the outside of the guide rails and pliers to hold the nylon lock nuts while you tighten them into the 5/8-inch countersunk holes.

    It has been revealed that the strap acts as a stop, limiting how far the legs can open. Wrap one end of an upholstery strap around the middle of the top cross brace (D) and staple it in place with a narrow-crown stapler. Open the stool until the seat sits level, then pull the strap snug and staple the other end centered on the underside of the top step (A). Use several 1/2-in. staples at each end so the strap holds securely.

    A step stool should be about 11 to 16-in. wide to fit both feet comfortably side by side. For a portable or compact version, stay toward the narrow end of that range.

    In a recent development, A single-step stool should be 6 to 9-in. tall. That’s a good height for reaching into a truck bed, helping kids reach a tall bathroom sink, or getting to the top pantry shelves.

    DAN ROBERTS FOR FAMILY HANDYMAN.

    What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

    📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (559 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk.
    • Industry observers note that shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore.
    • The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

    Industry observers note that shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”.

    The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is key before picking up a shovel.

    Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

    Industry observers note that heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

    Sources indicate that the added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

    The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

    Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

    Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is key even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

    Recent findings suggest that the American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

    It has been revealed that slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

    People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

    Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

    Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

    American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”.

    Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload.
    • Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space.
    • Sources indicate that the California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    According to recent reports, A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

    Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

    Sources indicate that the California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

    Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

    Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

    White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

    According to recent reports, but they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for swiftly loading or unloading goods.

    Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

    According to recent reports, green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

    Recent findings suggest that blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

    The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

    How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

    📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.
    • Industry observers note that with the average cost of a latest car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used.
    • Sources indicate that use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

    Industry observers note that with the average cost of a latest car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin says to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

    Sources indicate that use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin claims. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

    Check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin notes. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

    According to recent reports, vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

    Industry observers note that turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin says. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

    Flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”.

    Industry observers note that even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical concerns with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

    Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

    No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.

    #8495. Latest Update: What the Heck Happened To Regular Gear Shifts?

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1629 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Familyhandyman ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: What the Heck Happened To Regular Gear Shifts?

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Why ate regular gear shifts being replaced by increasingly impractical buttons and screens?
    • Sources indicate that you sit down in the driver’s seat of your car, push the start button, and then reach for the gear lever.
    • Recent findings suggest that there was a time when shifting gears was one of the most fundamental parts of driving.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Why ate regular gear shifts being replaced by increasingly impractical buttons and screens? Here's the deal.

    Sources indicate that you sit down in the driver’s seat of your car, push the start button, and then reach for the gear lever. Except it’s not there. The console has ten cup holders and three phone charging ports, but no gear shift. Nothing above it on the dash either: that’s also lever-lackin’. Upon the column like an old school pickup? Nope.

    Recent findings suggest that there was a time when shifting gears was one of the most fundamental parts of driving. You reached for a lever, moved it into position, and felt a mechanical connection between your hand and the machinery responsible for making the car move. Whether you drove a three-on-the-tree sedan, a four-speed muscle car, or a truck with a modern automatic, there was a lever involved in changing gears.

    Then automakers decided that shifting gears was probably too much work.

    In a recent development, today’s vehicles increasingly replace conventional gear selectors with things that are decidedly not gear selectors. Rotary knobs, push buttons, electronic switches, touchscreen menus, and all manner of non-levers are now in vogue.

    The question is simple: What happened to gear shifts, and why did automakers decide that one of the most recognizable controls in an automobile needed reinventing?

    Industry observers note that early automobiles required direct mechanical connections between the driver’s controls and the transmission. Whether automatic or manual, gearboxes used levers and linkages to move internal components into position to make the vehicle drive. The gear lever was a functional necessity.

    Sources indicate that as automatic transmissions became more common in the 1960s, the familiar PRND (Park, Reverse, Neutral, Drive) arrangement became standard. Whether mounted on the steering column or the center console, the selector offered a straightforward interface with an obvious purpose. And it was usually physically connected to what it was doing in the transmission.

    The mechanical connection also provided useful feedback. Moving a lever into Drive felt different from selecting Reverse or Park. The driver could often determine the selected gear by feel without looking down at the shifter.

    In a recent development, msst recently, however, electronic controls began replacing mechanical linkages. Known as shift-by-wire, these systems communicate the driver’s selection electronically rather than relying on a direct physical connection between the selector and transmission. By the 2010s this was the norm in consumer vehicles and the disconnection between driver and machine began in earnest.

    Recent findings suggest that this technology offered automakers more freedom in where and how they placed gear controls. It also opened the door to an increasingly strange assortment of alternatives. With the advent of increasingly smartphone-on-wheels designs, making the gear shift a radical part of design is now all the rage.

    In a recent development, once a conventional mechanical linkage was no longer necessary, designers gained considerable freedom. A rotary dial could perform the same function as a traditional lever. A collection of buttons could accomplish the same task. A small electronic toggle could select Drive or Reverse without occupying much space.

    Some manufacturers embraced the change enthusiastically.

    Industry observers note that jaguar Land Rover became particularly associated with rotary gear selectors, including the rising dial used in certain Jaguar and Land Rover models. Chrysler experimented with rotary selectors in vehicles such as the Ram 1500 (rapidly finding out that many truck owners hate them), while Ford and other manufacturers introduced electronic switches and compact selectors across portions of their lineups. Honda famously went to push buttons that were immediately compared to the (questionable, short-lived) push-button shifting American Motors used in the 1950s.

    In a recent development, mercedes-Benz moved many gear selectors to a steering-column stalk, freeing space on the center console. Not wanting to be left behind, Hyundai did the same, but with bulkier shifters located down low on the column. Others kept a traditional-appearing shifter, but made it barely move and difficult to shift into neutral (Nissan) or manual control (Subaru).

    Sources indicate that the reasoning isn’t entirely unreasonable. A conventional shifter can consume valuable cabin space, particularly in vehicles with complex center consoles. Replacing it with a dial or switch can free room for storage, cupholders, charging pads, and other amenities.

    Electronic selectors can also reduce the number of mechanical components required between the cabin and transmission.

    But there is a difference between making a control smaller and making it better.

    A conventional lever communicates something to the driver through its position and movement. A rotary dial or momentary switch often depends on a display or indicator to communicate the selected gear. The control becomes less self-explanatory, and the driver may need to look down to confirm what the vehicle is doing.

    Industry observers note that that isn’t necessarily a deal-breaker, but it raises an obvious question: What problem was the latest design solving for the person behind the wheel? This question often goes unanswered.

    Automotive interiors have become battlegrounds for designers seeking to make each new model feel more modern than the last. Large screens, minimalist dashboards, floating center consoles, and increasingly elaborate ambient lighting have become selling points. Traditional physical controls can appear old-fashioned in comparison.

    And despite design trends toward “minimalism” in vehicle cabins, prospective buyers are expecting more. We want cup holders capable of increasingly large volumes. We want phone chargers so we don’t have to plug anything in. We want a place to put a purse. An extra drink. Our miscellaneous devices. Car keys. A picture of grandma.

    Sources indicate that despite design trends pushing toward minimalism, American car buyers are anything but minimal with the amount of stuff we expect to fit in our cars. A current, full-sized pickup truck will have no fewer than six drink holders within the driver’s reach. Because that’s what focus groups demand. Holes in the center console for a purse? Yep, also demanded in most SUVs and minivans. Two or more wireless phone chargers? Also requested. Set-and-forget climate controls? Thumbs up there too. Plugs for dash cams, a place for the air freshener that isn’t the rearview, a way to get into the center storage bin from at least four of the vehicle’s seating positions, six ways to put… You get the idea. We want a lot. While being minimal. Because that aesthetic is in.

    It has been revealed that so the conventional gear lever became an option that could be eliminated to make more space for other stuff, while achieving a minimalist look. And so the gear shift… Well, shifted to somewhere else.

    Some of the alternatives make no sense whatsoever.

    The problem isn’t that electronic shifters are inherently bad. It’s that automakers sometimes appear to treat novelty as an improvement in itself. A control that performs the same task in a less intuitive way hasn’t necessarily advanced automotive technology. It may simply have changed the shape of the inconvenience.

    Much of the more recent change has come thanks to electric vehicles accelerating the transformation.

    Most battery-electric vehicles don’t use conventional multi-gear transmissions. Their electric motors can deliver useful torque across a broad operating range, allowing many EVs to operate with a single fixed reduction gear rather than the multiple forward ratios common in gasoline-powered vehicles.

    Drivers still need to select Park, Reverse, Neutral, and Drive, but there is less reason to retain a traditional transmission selector designed around a conventional automatic gearbox.

    Recent findings suggest that add in that many EVs have been just experimental smartphones with wheels, and things get even dicier. Early adopters of a new technology are usually happy to accept all kinds of radical changes and inconveniences for the privilege of being first. And so gear shifters got radicalized in electric cars.

    Industry observers note that some EVs use steering-column stalks. Others employ center-console switches, small toggles, or touchscreen controls. The absence of a conventional transmission also gives designers more freedom when arranging the cabin. Things could be sleeker, thinner, lower, and above all.. Whiter. Every early EV seemed to have a white interior with a complete absence of useful buttons or switches. Giant TV-sized screens dominated the interior instead.

    However, electrification doesn’t automatically justify every unusual design. An EV still needs a clear, accessible way to select a direction of travel. The motor may be simpler than a conventional powertrain, but the driver’s task remains fundamentally the same: choose where the vehicle should go.

    Industry observers note that slowly, as EVs gained mainstream appeal, those “old school” controls began to return. Today, the best-selling electrics for any given carmaker are usually the ones that are cars that happen to be electric rather than being electric for EV sake.

    Industry observers note that probably not everywhere, but it isn’t disappearing entirely. In fact, it’s making a bit of a comeback. It’s the traditional manual transmission that is becoming rarer than an uncirculated wheat penny. Among automatic vehicles, some manufacturers retain conventional-looking selectors because customers understand them and find them comfortable to use. And a few of those manufacturers who deviated are coming back to them.

    According to recent reports, the likely future is a mixture of approaches. Electronic shift-by-wire technology will remain in nearly all vehicles because it offers packaging flexibility and integrates readily with modern vehicle electronics. And is less likely to break. EVs will likely continue to use compact selectors, while performance cars and pickup trucks may preserve more traditional controls where they contribute to driver engagement.

    The crucial distinction is between modernizing a control and needlessly complicating it.

    Perhaps that’s what the industry has forgotten: The best automotive controls aren’t always the newest or the smallest. They’re the ones that do their jobs so well that the driver barely has to think about them.

    #8494. Judge Richard Posner, RIP

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1027 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Reason ↗ Open Full Page

    Judge Richard Posner, RIP

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that judge Richard Posner passed away yesterday.
    • Industry observers note that as a longtime professor at the University of Chicago Law School, Posner was a pioneer of the application of economics to legal complications.
    • Recent findings suggest that in addition to his many contributions to law and economics, Posner also published enormously influential books and articles on a dizzying array of other concerns.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that judge Richard Posner passed away yesterday. Posner was one of the greatest legal scholars of all time, one of the founders of the field of law and economics, and probably the most influential lower-court federal judge of the last several decades. His contributions across a wide range of fields are so great, that no obituary can possibly do them justice.

    Industry observers note that as a longtime professor at the University of Chicago Law School, Posner was a pioneer of the application of economics to legal complications. His book Economic Analysis of Law, (which has gone through numerous editions since the first one in 1973), was and is the best overview of the field. His classic articles on antitrust law, regulation, the economics of common law, and many related issues were pathbreaking applications of economics to law that continue to influence economists, legal scholars, and policymakers even many decades later.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to his many contributions to law and economics, Posner also published enormously influential books and articles on a dizzying array of other concerns. I can only mention a few here. His book Sex and Reason is a tremendously insightful analysis of legal regulation of intimate relationships. How Judges Think and Reflections on Judging shed light on a variety of issues relating to judicial behavior, and legal philosophy. Law and Literature is one of the greatest books on the depiction of law in classic literary works. This list of pathbreaking Posner works can be extended almost endlessly!

    Posner became a federal appellate judge in 1981 (appointed to the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit). There, he became perhaps the most influential federal lower court judge of his time, writing a variety of widely cited opinions. He was famous in legal circles for drafting almost all of his opinions himself, rarely relying on law clerks to do it.

    A few of my own experiences with Posner and his work may shed some small additional light on the man and his achievements.

    In a recent development, as a first-year law student, I was required to take an early-morning Contracts class. Not being a morning person, I periodically overslept and missed class (Posner, I'm sure, would never have done such a thing!). As a result, I was confused about some issues when final exam time came around. The class textbook was only of limited help in clearing up my confusion. So I decided to read the contracts chapter of Economic Analysis of Law. In a relatively few pages, Posner made everything much clearer, and I came to a much better understanding of a wide range of contracts issues than I had before, from studying the much longer textbook. Thanks to Posner, I did much better on the exam than I had any right to expect. He had a gift for distilling complex issues of law and public policy and making them readily understandable even to late-sleeping slackers!

    Recent findings suggest that A few years later, I was a law clerk for a federal appellate judge. Usually, when courts cite legal precedents, they do not indicate the name of the judge who wrote the decision. But my judge - who is more conservative than Posner and has a very different judicial philosophy - made clear that, when citing a Posner opinion, I should make sure to indicate Posner was the author. It's a small, but telling, indication of the respect Posner commanded from jurists across the political and jurisprudential spectrum.

    Early in my academic career, I was co-editor of the Supreme Court Economic Review. One of the more difficult duties of academic journal editors is dealing with peer reviewers, who often procrastinate,  submit inadequate reviews, or both. One time, on a Friday afternoon, I e-mailed Posner an article submission, asking him to review it. Due to his simultaneous work as legal scholar and judge, Posner was almost certainly much busier than most of our other reviewers. Still, on Saturday morning, I woke up to find a message from Posner in my e-mail inbox. I expected the message would indicate whether he accepted the assignment or not. But instead, I found an extremely thorough and insightful review of the article I had sent him - one of the best peer review reports I have ever seen. In addition to his many other achievements and talents, Posner was extraordinarily hard-working and efficient. He made most of the rest of us seem lazy and indolent by comparison.

    Industry observers note that I was privileged to know Posner over a period of many years, though we interacted only occasionally. Most of my professional writings related to his work were critical, as in the case of my review of his book Law, Pragmatism, and Democracy, (to which he wrote a solid response,  and I in turn did a short rejoinder), and my criticism (in my book The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of Latest London and the Limits of Eminent Domain) of his defense of the Supreme Court's controversial ruling in Kelo v. City of New London.

    It has been revealed that in retrospect, I fear these writings did not always sufficiently convey the enormous respect - even awe - that I had for Posner's many achievements. But I did support his longstanding campaign to get rid of the Bluebook, the ridiculously overcomplicated system of legal citation. In general, I am not a fan of book-burning. But I was happy to follow Posner in making an exception for the Bluebook! For a time, we even collaborated on an effort to persuade law journal editors to rethink the system.

    Much, much more can be noted. No words of mine can even come close to doing justice to Judge Posner's many achievements, or to his generosity to students and younger colleagues, of which my own experiences with him were just small examples. Thus, I will close by offering my profound condolences to those of his friends, family, and colleagues, who might read this post.

    ENHANCEMENT: For more on Judge Posner's life and achievements, see this obituary on the University of Chicago Law School website.

    If You See Cyan Lights on a Car, Here’s What They Mean

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars.
    • Colored lights play an important part in driving safety.
    • Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    Cyan lights could soon appear on more self-driving cars. Here's what the unusual color means and why federal regulators want to standardize it.

    Colored lights play an important part in driving safety. Red brake lights mean a vehicle is slowing down, amber turn signals indicate someone is turning, flashing red and blue indicate an emergency, and yellow lights can mean a hazard or warning.

    But what about cyan? Drivers might be noticing that color more often in the future as the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently proposed new federal standards for these lights as automated vehicles become more common.

    Learn what the color would mean, where it’s already appearing, and what drivers should expect in the future.

    Industry observers note that cyan lights would indicate that a vehicle’s automated driving system is in control and no one inside needs to actively monitor the road. The lights could appear on cars with someone behind the wheel or vehicles that operate without a human driver.

    Industry observers note that on Oct. 23, NHTSA unveiled a proposal to establish federal standards for these lights, including their placement and brightness. The lights would remain steady rather than flash, and drivers would be able to see them from all sides of the vehicle. The proposal is part of a broader effort to update safety requirements for automated vehicles, including those NHTSA describes as “vehicles designed never to be driven by a human being.”.

    Sources indicate that “As automotive technology continues to evolve, our safety standards must keep pace with innovation in ways that do not compromise public safety,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison mentioned in the agency’s release. “These proposed updates address unnecessary regulatory burdens for vehicles built without traditional manual controls while establishing clear performance standards for automated vehicle marker lamps. By aligning our regulations with today’s technology, we are paving the way for safe innovation and setting clear rules of the road for automated vehicles.”.

    In a recent development, cyan would help other drivers, pedestrians, and law enforcement recognize when an automated system is handling the driving. Unlike common driver-assistance features that help with steering or speed, these systems can operate without constant human supervision under certain conditions.

    The lights wouldn’t give self-driving cars any special privileges or change how other drivers should behave around them.

    According to recent reports, mercedes-Benz has already received permission to use turquoise-colored lights on certain vehicles in California and Nevada. California approved testing on freeways, while Nevada allowed the lights on certain production vehicles.

    The lights work with Mercedes-Benz’s Drive Pilot system, which can handle driving under specific conditions. A driver still needs to remain available to take control when requested. The tech giant has tested the lights near the outside mirrors and on the front and rear of its vehicles.

    “Mercedes-Benz is committed to standardizing the color turquoise,” the tech giant remarked in a release, explaining that the goal is to make automated driving systems easier for people to recognize around the world.

    Recent findings suggest that those approvals came before NHTSA’s latest proposal, which could establish a consistent standard for other manufacturers across the country. For now, the new federal rules are still under consideration. Even if NHTSA finalizes them, carmakers wouldn’t have to install cyan lights on self-driving vehicles. Manufacturers that choose to use them would need to follow the new standards.

    Under the proposal, the lights could turn on when the automated system is driving without someone monitoring the road. They’d have to turn off when a person is expected to resume that responsibility. Drivers wouldn’t need to do anything differently when they see cyan lights, but they’d have a clearer idea of who’s controlling the vehicle.

    National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, “Trump’s Transportation Department Makes Commonsense Updates to Vehicle Lighting Standards for AVs”.

    That Hole in Your Ruler Isn’t Random – Here’s What It’s Actually For

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history.
    • Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line.
    • Recent findings suggest that those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    That small hole on a ruler has a practical purpose and an unexpected history. Here's why it exists and how people use it.

    Almost everyone has used a ruler at some point, whether it was for a school project, measuring something around the house, or drawing a straight line. But even after years of using one, there’s a small detail that’s easy to miss: the hole near the end.

    Recent findings suggest that those holes in rulers aren’t just part of the design. They actually serve a purpose, and the reason they’re there goes back further than most people might expect. Here’s what they’re for, how they were used in the past, and a few other ways they come in handy.

    According to recent reports, the hole at the end of a ruler is mainly there for storage. It lets people hang the ruler on a hook, nail, or pegboard instead of leaving it in a drawer or on a workbench. This is particularly helpful with longer metal rulers that might not fit in a toolbox.

    But the hole has been around for much longer than modern workshops. Years ago, before paper notebooks became common in schools, students practiced writing on small slate boards. They could wipe away their writing with a damp cloth and use the board again.

    Some students tied that cloth to their rulers with a piece of string through the hole. That way, they always had something nearby to clean their slates. Schools eventually moved away from slate boards, but the holes remained. Today, they’re mostly there to make rulers easier to hang and store.

    According to recent reports, hanging a ruler isn’t the only reason manufacturers add holes. Some rulers have several, and they can serve different purposes depending on where they’re placed. For example, certain school rulers have three holes spaced along one side. These line up with the rings in a standard three-ring binder, so students can keep their rulers with their other school supplies.

    Some rulers also have holes that help with drawing circles. A pin through one hole can hold the ruler in place while a pencil in another hole traces a circle as the ruler turns. Not every ruler has holes designed for this, but specialty models like the Creative Grids Quick Trim Ruler do. A compass is still a better choice when exact measurements matter.

    Some crafting rulers have holes for more specific jobs. Quilting rulers and templates may have openings that help mark circles or line up fabric before cutting. Others have slots or shaped edges that guide a rotary cutter, making it easier to cut certain shapes.

    There are also special rulers for paper crafts and stitching. Some have rows of tiny, evenly spaced holes that help people mark where to make stitches or decorative patterns.

    Of course, not every ruler has holes. Smaller plastic rulers often don’t need them, while longer metal versions may have one at each end. It mostly comes down to how the manufacturer expects people to use the ruler. And for everyday measuring, the holes don’t make much difference. A ruler without them can measure just as accurately as one with them.

    #8488. Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

    📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (641 w)

    Winter Storm Watch vs. Winter Storm Warning: What’s the Difference?

    📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things.
    • In a recent development, tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology.
    • According to recent reports, both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

    A winter storm watch and winter storm warning mean different things. Here's what each alert signals and how to prepare for dangerous weather.

    In a recent development, tracking severe weather can sometimes feel like it requires a degree in meteorology. With complex scientific terms and technical jargon, it can be difficult to understand what it all means and what should be done to prepare. That’s when the difference between a winter storm watch and a winter storm warning matters.

    According to recent reports, both alerts come from the National Weather Service, but they call for different levels of urgency. Here’s how the alerts work and what homeowners should do when they see one.

    It has been revealed that A winter storm watch means a significant winter storm is possible, but forecasters aren’t yet sure where or when it will hit or how severe it will be. According to the National Weather Service, watches often arrive a day or two before a storm and can cover heavy snow, sleet, or ice.

    Recent findings suggest that they give residents time to prepare, even though the storm may not reach their area. As the forecast becomes clearer, the National Weather Service may upgrade the watch to a warning, matter an advisory, or cancel it altogether.

    A winter storm warning means dangerous winter weather is expected or already happening. Heavy snow, sleet, or ice could make travel unsafe and cause other problems, including power outages. The amount of snow or ice needed to trigger a warning varies by location.

    Sources indicate that “Each office knows the local area and will matter Warnings, Watches or Advisories based on local criteria,” according to the National Weather Service. “For example, the amount of snow that triggers a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Northern Plains is typically much higher than the amount needed to trigger a ‘Winter Storm Warning’ in the Southeast.”.

    Warnings generally arrive closer to a storm’s arrival than watches, although forecasters can issue one before snow or ice begins falling.

    A winter weather advisory means snow, sleet, or ice is expected to cause problems, but forecasters don’t anticipate conditions severe enough for a warning. An advisory may signal slick roads or other travel disruptions. While the weather may be less severe than during a warning, residents should still take precautions and monitor local forecasts.

    A winter storm watch gives homeowners time to prepare before conditions worsen. That includes checking heating systems, protecting exposed pipes from freezing, and stocking up on food, medications, and other essentials.

    “Your primary concerns at home or work during a winter storm are loss of heat, power and telephone service and a shortage of supplies if storm conditions continue for more than a day,” according to the National Weather Service.

    Homeowners should have flashlights, spare batteries, and a charged phone in case the power goes out. Checking smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locating snow shovels, and stocking up on ice melt can also help.

    Once a warning takes effect, homeowners should finish their preparations and avoid unnecessary travel. Staying indoors is generally safest during severe winter weather.

    If the power goes out, residents can close off unused rooms and wear extra layers to stay warm. Portable generators should always remain outdoors, away from windows and doors. Grills and ovens should never serve as heating sources because they can create serious safety hazards.

    Residents should continue monitoring weather alerts throughout the storm. Once conditions improve, homeowners can check for damage and begin clearing snow and ice from walkways and driveways.

    Sources indicate that national Weather Service, “Winter Weather Warnings, Watches and Advisories” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Resources and Frequently Asked Questions” National Weather Service, “Prepare! Don’t Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise” Federal Emergency Management Agency, “Be Prepared for a Winter Storm”.
